edits.anchor: The alternation between hot and cold has been a fixture of Nordic bathing culture for centuries and sports medicine for decades. The basic mechanism isn't complicated: hot water opens the blood vessels and relaxes the muscles; cold water closes them; the body's response to cycling between the two has cardiovascular benefits that some researchers associate with improved circulation, reduced fatigue, and a significant mood lift in the hours that follow. The science is still accumulating (this isn't medical advice, and individual experience varies), but the physiological story is at least coherent.

There's no single right order. Some people start in the cedar sauna, which runs hotter and drier than the hot tub, then move to the cold creek off the dock, then settle into the hot tub as a warm recovery stage. Some skip the sauna and just cycle between the hot tub and the creek. Both work. The rule is to stay long enough in each direction that the contrast lands: ten minutes in, two minutes out, repeat until the world has recalibrated.
edits.after:
Here's how I run it: fifteen minutes in the cedar sauna, two minutes in the creek, ten minutes in the hot tub, then back to the creek for two more minutes to finish. Sauna first, because the dry heat gets all the way into my shoulders in a way the hot tub doesn't. The creek is the reset in between; two minutes is my number, though anywhere from one to three minutes is plenty once the water's dropped below 60 degrees or so, since the cold does its work fast. Then the hot tub for ten minutes, to let the heat settle all the way back in. And the creek again at the end: that's the part I don't skip.

Ending cold, rather than climbing back into the hot tub after, seems to be where the real payoff sits. Some research links cold water immersion to a release of norepinephrine and endorphins and a lift in mood and alertness that outlasts the initial shock, and that lift seems to need the cold to be the last thing your body feels before you let it warm back up on its own.
